messages.subject: Problem with secr.fit
messages.subject_clean: Problem with secr.fit
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I have run into some problems with my model. It's a data set of American black bears hair snagged over a summer using baited detectors. This was divided into 4 occasions. Each occasion lasted 12 days except the 4th, which ran 22 days. I specified that in the Detection location text file as:

#Detector X Y Effort
5 497786 5379253 12 12 12 22
6 500922 5379112 12 12 12 22
#

We are interested in obtain density estimates for male and female bears, so we divided the capture histories as such.
Our study area was also a peninsula, so bears could walk off our trapping area on only 1 narrow stretch. The rest of the study area was bounded by lakes.
We built a habitat mask using the following code:
#
female.mask=make.mask(femaletrap,type="polygon",poly=Voya[],check.poly=T)
#
where femaletrap was the female traps object (using code: traps(femalecapthist)) and Voya is our shapefile (read in using readShapePoly)

Earlier we were specifying a buffer in the make.mask object, but now realize that we don't need this.

When we plotted the mask it seemed like all the mask points were nicely distributed over the land area excluding the water.

We then tried to run a null model with the following code:
#
null.f=secr.fit(females,mask=female.mask,CL=F)
#
But got the following warnings:
1: In secr.fit(females, mask = female.mask, CL = F) :
  possible maximization error: nlm returned code 3. See ?nlm
2: In secr.fit(females, mask = female.mask, CL = F) :
  at least one variance calculation failed

We also attempted detection as a function of time with the following code:
#
t.f=secr.fit(females,g0~t,mask=female.mask,CL=F)
#
But the following warning was given:
In secr.fit(females, g0 ~ t, mask = female.mask, CL = F) :
  possible maximization error: nlm returned code 3. See ?nlm

We have run our data for males using the same code and mask and seem to have no issues.

I would be grateful for any information/help/material you could provide.
Roshan.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Roshan
The error messages are fairly general, so it's hard to know what to suggest. Often the nlm code 3 message can be ignored, but in this case you are missing at least one variance, so it's worth pressing on.  It's worth double checking the data entry with plot(females, tracks = TRUE) and summary(females). Otherwise all I can suggest is trying some variations in the call to secr.fit: method = 'Nelder-Mead' is a good start. Also try overriding the usage data with details = list(ignoreusage = TRUE). I suspect you don't really need to allow for varying usage.
Murray

Yes, and nice to feel it yielded to a collective effort!

Follow-up points:

I think Roshan accidentally pasted the same output twice for males and females, but at least the numbers look healthy. The female plot, I'm not so sure. That large return movement to the west has me worried, and is definitely worth checking in the raw data. Even if correct, it is an outlier that has the potential to trip up the analysis (with a halfnormal detection function the probability of such an extreme is very small; an exponential function may be more accommodating).

In 'secr' we use a numerical algorithm to find the combination of parameter values that maximizes the likelihood. The default algorithm (Newton-Raphson in nlm) repeatedly approximates the gradient of the multidimensional surface and heads 'uphill'. Nelder-Mead is another algorithm widely liked for its robustness, although it is somewhat slower and requires an extra step at the end to estimate the variances. The Wikipedia entry is somewhat negative, but it generally works. See also ?optim, where it is the default method. When everything goes well, both methods give essentially the same answer.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hello secr users,
I have genetic data from coyote and red fox scat data collected over 2 winters. The scats were collected in an opportunistic fashion while doing snow tracking surveys. We did not define strict sampling areas prior to beginning collections. Basically, while moving around our general study region counting tracks, we would collect any scats that we came across. My question is about choosing the correct detector method to use for this type of data. Currently, I am experimenting with the polygon detector type. I have drawn several polygons around the main clusters of scat locations, and have done so in such a way that I am confident that sampling intensity was consistent within each polygon. Is this type of post hoc detector selection appropriate? If not, can you suggest an alternative? Thanks

Casey

messages.body_plain:
Hi Casey

A purist might say "these data lack the spatial control needed for analysis, don't do it", but that might waste some good, if imperfect, data. I think the key problem is not what you should do, but how you are going to convince a sceptical reader or reviewer. There is obvious potential for bias if you narrow the nominal search polygons down to places you found scat, as then no such polygon can be empty. This risk gets less as you zoom out and blur the boundaries, so I would tend toward delineating the largest polygons in which you felt scats might have been found (if you had wandered differently on the day). My comment about convincing sceptics leads on to the idea that you might need to simulate the effect on estimates of various polygon-construction rules. That's more work, but at least you'll be warm and dry in the office, and perhaps it's the price you pay... It might be hard to design convincing simulations as you have to capture the possible bias in your sampling.

As you might have noticed from other posts, I'm not so sure the strict 'polygon' detector types are the best solution because they require some special integration code in secr that I have not used much myself. The alternative is to discretize the searched area as a set of pixels (grid squares) and treat each as a point (proximity) detector located at its centre. If you use no more than a few hundred pixels this is likely to be faster and give essentially the same answer.

I'll be interested to hear what Eric has to say on this.

Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Casey et al.

I was happy to see this post, as we have been dealing with a similar situation.  Scats were collected opportunistically throughout a large (> 600 sqkm) study area.  Searching for scats was the main focus of field work, but a systematic survey design was not established prior to collecting the data.  GPS track logs were not used to delineate areas searched, however, records were kept describing whether or not, and how many times, any part of each (1km X 1km) cell in a grid covering the entire study area was visited while searching for scat.  The majority of cells were never searched, and there were many cells that were searched but where no scat was found. We defined post hoc search area polygons (polygon detector type, with detections modeled as counts during a single survey rather than as binary data within sampling occasions) as the perimeters of searched grid cells (in the case where adjacent cells were not searched), and as the perimeters of aggregations of cells where >1 adjacent cells were searched at least once.  This is different than Murray's suggestion of treating the centroid of each searched cell as a proximity detector, but might result in a very similar detection model if cells were sized appropriately (??)).  In short, because field staff recorded the cells that they searched within on each day that they searched, we were able to describe (approximately) the spatial distribution of search effort across the greater study area in the model.  Might there be any way you can recover similar information?

We also looked at merged buffers around individual samples collected, and MCPs around all, and around clusters of, collected samples as ways to approximate the area searched in an SECR model with polygon detectors.  Buffered areas were smaller than the search area polygons defined as described above because they excluded areas that were searched but no scat was found. MCPs were generally larger, because they included large areas between sample collection locations that were never actually searched.  We suspect that using a buffer or MCP around locations where samples were actually collected as the search area polygons could have introduced bias, in the first case (buffers - similar to your initial approach I think) because it would appear that samples were found everywhere they were searched for, and in the second case (MCPs) because it would appear as though large areas that were searched yielded no detections when in fact they were never searched.  We therefore preferred to use the perimeter of searched grid cells to define the the search area polygons, even though this is only an approximation because entire cells were not necessarily searched.  We were fortunate to have the gridded data describing search effort.  Casey, if you go with the polygon detector type, it might be useful to try to discriminate between areas where you might have found scat but didn't vs. those where you couldn't have found scat even if it was there.  Include all areas where you might have found scat if it was there (because you were walking and not driving? or because you were walking and not too busy to notice and collect scat?) as (part of) a search area polygon, and exclude other areas from search area polygons.  This would ensure your polygon detectors allow for the fact that some areas yielded no samples even though you "searched" there, whereas others yielded no samples because you didn't search there.

A second issue we had to deal with was the fact that (parts of) some cells were searched a large number of times, whereas other cells were searched rarely or only once.  We did have the data describing the number of times each cell was visited, so we were able to model variation in search effort among search area polygons using the method described in Efford, Borchers and Mowat (2013) and implemented in the secr package as the 'effort' attribute of the traps object.  We defined effort as the number of times a cell was visited for single-cell polygons, and as the mean number of times each cell in multi-cell polygons was visited.  We obtained lower AICc values and different density estimates when we modeled the variation in search effort across search area polygons vs. when we ignored it, and will present only estimates where we modeled the variation.

A third issue was severe habitat heterogeneity.  Forests comprised about 17% of the greater study area, distributed in fairly small fragments throughout it.  Animals relied on the forest fragments and all samples were collected in forests.  Therefore, (1) although we defined areas searched as (aggregations of) square 1km X 1km grid cells, only the forest fragments within these cells would have been searched; and (2) if areas searched contained a higher proportion of forest than areas not searched, we would overestimate population size on the greater study area if we ignored habitat heterogeneity and also extrapolated densities estimated from data collected on the areas searched across the greater study area. We therefore used spatial data describing forest cover to build the habitat masks used for density and population size estimation.  Density estimates were therefore specific to forested areas within and in the vicinity of the areas searched.  We assumed that density in forest fragments outside the areas searched was similar, and extrapolated across forested habitat within the greater study area to estimate population size (using the region.N function).  Because it was of interest for comparing with results of other studies, we also estimated density "across the fragmented landscape", i.e. assuming homogeneous habitat, using a mask with uniform point spacing throughout.  The associated density estimate was, as expected, much lower.  For my own interest, I estimated population size assuming habitat homogeneity, and the estimate was considerably higher than where we used the forest cover data to define areas where activity centers could occur.  I suspect this was because areas searched included a higher proportion of forest than the greater study area on average.  These differences may not be relevant to your study if you sampled within a large expanse of contiguous habitat, but it's always a good idea to carefully consider the area across which you extrapolate your density estimates if you estimate population size using "region.N".  Areas where activity centers could not occur (e.g. large bodies of water, cleared, built-up or urban areas) should usually be excluded from masks used for population size estimation, for example if you only searched for scat in areas used by foxes, but the greater study area includes areas not used by them.

Casey, I realize that this may not be very useful to you if you really have no data describing areas that you searched but found no samples, or have no information about areas/habitat types that foxes use vs those they don't.  Maybe it will help to see how we tried to cope with a somewhat similar situation ("opportunistic" fecal sampling with no a priori survey design), using the data available.

Our manuscript has not been submitted yet, but there's potential for reviewers to poke holes in how we used our data to fit an SECR model when really samples were not collected following a specific design required by the models.  I'd be grateful to hear any thoughts or comments about the approach we took, or about the general feasibility of "mashing" data from "opportunistically" or "haphazardly" collected scat into an SECR model.

All the best,
Eric

Great stuff, Eric. I don't have your knowledge based on detailed examination of a real example, but I'll emphasise a couple of points from your main post. Your third issue relates to an Achilles heel of the SECR approach when the real concern is total number: what you get depends very much on the extent of suitable habitat and how you have sampled this. I don't rule out that non-spatial CR may be better in some cases.

And re-stating the obvious: if you (Casey) are going to make an arbitrary decision in the analysis to make up for weak data collection then you really need to present a spectrum of analyses to show how the decision impacts (or ideally does not impact) on the results. Appendices and online supplements were made for this!

To avoid confusion: the relevant attribute in secr is called 'usage' not 'effort'. Also, 'mash' is a technical term in secr with a meaning different to Eric's 'mashing' ;-)  I ran out of words one day...

Murray

We therefore preferred to use the perimeter of searched grid cells to define the the search area polygons, even though this is only an approximation because entire cells were not necessarily searched.  We were fortunate to have the gridded data describing search effort.  Casey, if you go with the polygon detector type, it might be useful to try to discriminate between areas where you might have found scat but didn't vs. those where you couldn't have found scat even if it was there.  Include all areas where you might have found scat if it was there (because you were walking and not driving? or because you were walking and not too busy to notice and collect scat?) as (part of) a search area polygon, and exclude other areas from search area polygons.  This would ensure your polygon detectors allow for the fact that some areas yielded no samples even though you "searched" there, whereas others yielded no samples because you didn't search there.
>
> A second issue we had to deal with was the fact that (parts of) some cells were searched a large number of times, whereas other cells were searched rarely or only once.  We did have the data describing the number of times each cell was visited, so we were able to model variation in search effort among search area polygons using the method described in Efford, Borchers and Mowat (2013) and implemented in the secr package as the 'effort' attribute of the traps object.  We defined effort as the number of times a cell was visited for single-cell polygons, and as the mean number of times each cell in multi-cell polygons was visited.  We obtained lower AICc values and different density estimates when we modeled the variation in search effort across search area polygons vs. when we ignored it, and will present only estimates where we modeled the variation.
>
> A third issue was severe habitat heterogeneity.  Forests comprised about 17% of the greater study area, distributed in fairly small fragments throughout it.  Animals relied on the forest fragments and all samples were collected in forests.  Therefore, (1) although we defined areas searched as (aggregations of) square 1km X 1km grid cells, only the forest fragments within these cells would have been searched; and (2) if areas searched contained a higher proportion of forest than areas not searched, we would overestimate population size on the greater study area if we ignored habitat heterogeneity and also extrapolated densities estimated from data collected on the areas searched across the greater study area. We therefore used spatial data describing forest cover to build the habitat masks used for density and population size estimation.  Density estimates were therefore specific to forested areas within and in the vicinity of the areas searched.  We assumed that density in forest fragments outside the areas searched was similar, and extrapolated across forested habitat within the greater study area to estimate population size (using the region.N function).  Because it was of interest for comparing with results of other studies, we also estimated density "across the fragmented landscape", i.e. assuming homogeneous habitat, using a mask with uniform point spacing throughout.  The associated density estimate was, as expected, much lower.  For my own interest, I estimated population size assuming habitat homogeneity, and the estimate was considerably higher than where we used the forest cover data to define areas where activity centers could occur.  I suspect this was because areas searched included a higher proportion of forest than the greater study area on average.  These differences may not be relevant to your study if you sampled within a large expanse of contiguous habitat, but it's always a good idea to carefully consider the area across which you extrapolate your density estimates if you estimate population size using "region.N".  Areas where activity centers could not occur (e.g. large bodies of water, cleared, built-up or urban areas) should usually be excluded from masks used for population size estimation, for example if you only searched for scat in areas used by foxes, but the greater study area includes areas not used by them.
>
> Casey, I realize that this may not be very useful to you if you really have no data describing areas that you searched but found no samples, or have no information about areas/habitat types that foxes use vs those they don't.  Maybe it will help to see how we tried to cope with a somewhat similar situation ("opportunistic" fecal sampling with no a priori survey design), using the data available.
>
> Our manuscript has not been submitted yet, but there's potential for reviewers to poke holes in how we used our data to fit an SECR model when really samples were not collected following a specific design required by the models.  I'd be grateful to hear any thoughts or comments about the approach we took, or about the general feasibility of "mashing" data from "opportunistically" or "haphazardly" collected scat into an SECR model.
>
> All the best,
> Eric

messages.body_plain:
I'm seeking some feedback on some observations regarding compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models.  I came across
Howe et al. 2013 yesterday which shows strong evidence for heterogeneity in g0 and sigma and modelling this heterogeneity as finite mixtures substantially raises estimated densities.  The link to that paper is here:

http://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10144-013-0389-y

In light of Murray's recent paper on compensatory heterogeneity, I thought I'd compare finite mixture models using the different parameterizations on some male black bear SCR data I have.  Murray's paper can be found here:

http://www.otago.ac.nz/density/pdfs/Efford%20and%20Mowat%202014%20Ecology.pdf

My initial thought was that we can test for non-compensatory heterogeneity in g0 using the a0 parameterization and it may be that Howe et al. could have gotten by using only a finite mixture on sigma and the a0 parameterization.  Here is an AIC table for a model without heterogeneity and 5 possible ways to model heterogeneity.  I've varied starting values and can't get different estimates, so I don't think any of these are at a local maxima and the mixture proportions aren't estimated on a boundary for any of these models.

                                                 model   detectfn npar    logLik      AIC     AICc  dAICc AICcwt
modMh5 D~Area a0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal   10 -1158.844 2337.687 2340.105  0.000 0.8268
modMh4      D~Area a0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1162.646 2343.292 2345.248  5.143 0.0632
modMh1      D~Area g0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1162.706 2343.412 2345.368  5.263 0.0595
modMh3 D~Area g0~Area + bk + h2 sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal   10 -1162.002 2344.003 2346.421  6.316 0.0351
modMh6      D~Area a0~Area + bk sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1164.063 2346.125 2348.082  7.977 0.0153
modMh2      D~Area g0~Area + bk sigma~Area + h2 pmix~h2 halfnormal    9 -1168.716 2355.432 2357.388 17.283 0.0000
modM                     D~Area g0~Area + bk sigma~Area halfnormal    7 -1183.127 2380.254 2381.446 41.341 0.0000

We see that 1) Heterogeneity of some sort is strongly supported, 2) the best g0 parameterization has a finite mixture on both g0 and sigma as in Howe et al., 3) among the models with a finite mixture on sigma alone, the one with compensatory heterogeneity on a0 is strongly preferred (modMh2 vs. modMh6), 4)  the two models with a finite mixture on either a0 or g0 alone are nearly indistinguishable and 5)  The model with finite mixtures on a0 and sigma is strongly preferred, suggesting non-compensatory heterogeneity on a0.

Now, let's look at the estimates and standard errors for N at one of the sites.

M:  64 (10)
Mh1:  106 (47)
Mh2:  155 (38)
Mh3:  200 (85)
Mh4:  108 (43)
Mh5:  79 (18)
Mh6:  55 (9)

We see that 1) The compensatory heterogeneity model (Mh6) produces a slightly lower estimate as the base model (M) with a similar standard error.  This seems consistent with Murray's points about what happens when you ignore heterogeneity that is compensatory.  2)  The top model with non-compensatory heterogeneity (Mh5) produces estimates that are slightly higher than the base model (M) but the standard error is much larger.  3)  The model fit by Howe et al. (Mh3) has produces a very large and imprecise estimate, but luckily, it doesn't carry much support.  Should we expect the estimates from models Mh5 and Mh3 to differ this greatly?

Let's look at the coefficients of these two models to see what is going on:

> coef(modMh5)
                   beta    SE.beta        lcl         ucl
D            -6.4536772 0.24774184 -6.9392423 -5.96811207
D.AreaPB     -0.5528546 0.25927280 -1.0610199 -0.04468924
a0            6.0425960 0.16944474  5.7104904  6.37470157
a0.AreaPB    -0.6834435 0.26055073 -1.1941135 -0.17277344
a0.bk         1.0841709 0.18395220  0.7236312  1.44471058
a0.h22       -1.2594503 0.36813108 -1.9809740 -0.53792665
sigma         8.0558197 0.09371943  7.8721330  8.23950644
sigma.AreaPB -0.5720924 0.13259523 -0.8319743 -0.31221055
sigma.h22     0.9389699 0.24047476  0.4676480  1.41029177
pmix.h22      1.0072750 0.37571976  0.2708778  1.74367221

> coef(modMh3)
                   beta   SE.beta        lcl          ucl
D            -5.9757480 0.3957638 -6.7514309 -5.200065229
D.AreaPB     -0.1057174 0.2684513 -0.6318723  0.420437443
g0           -2.6879640 0.1724324 -3.0259254 -2.350002747
g0.AreaPB    -0.1776700 0.2549628 -0.6773880  0.322047930
g0.bk         1.2809791 0.1896395  0.9092925  1.652665767
g0.h22       -1.5156360 0.5264688 -2.5474959 -0.483776057
sigma         8.1066234 0.1014152  7.9078531  8.305393563
sigma.AreaPB -0.2620560 0.1308774 -0.5185710 -0.005540901
sigma.h22    -0.6996332 0.3035928 -1.2946641 -0.104602325
pmix.h22      1.8856367 0.4507021  1.0022767  2.768996601

The a0 parameterization has the second mixture group increasing sigma, but reducing a0, which implies g0 is reduced, and more than you would expect with compensatory heterogeneity.  The g0 parameterization has the second group decreasing both sigma and g0, or conversely, the first group increases g0 as you increase sigma, the same pattern observed by Howe et al., the opposite of what is observed using a0, and completely inconsistent with compensatory heterogeneity.

This leads me wondering 1)  Maybe the a0 parameterization is better for modelling individual heterogeneity and Howe et al. may find that this model fits their data better, produces lower and less variable estimates, and their cause for concern about modelling individual heterogeneity was perhaps exaggerated, 2) maybe we need to allow for different mixture proportions on the two parameters, or 3) these finite mixture models are just not reliable, or at least not reliable with my small data set.

A just so story for my top model is that we sampled during breeding season so subordinate males moved more than dominant  males (larger sigma) and subordinate males are smaller so they tend to leave less hair in the hair snares (lower g0).  I'm sure I could think of some more!

Thoughts?

Thanks for your time (if you made it this far!),

Ben Augustine

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ben,

In Howe et al. (2013), we presented results for females only.  If you are analyzing a data set that includes both sexes, then I wouldn't expect the patterns of variation in SECR model parameters to be similar, as sex is likely a large source of the individual heterogeneity (especially in sigma) in your data set.  As I understand it, the a0 formulation and a two-point mixture distribution is well-suited for the case where there are large differences in home range size, but small or no differences in probability of detection for individuals with activity centers at a detector, between two groups of individuals (often sexes), but group membership is not observed (i.e. sex is unknown).  If this is the case with your data, I don't see specific reasons to suspect problems with results from your a0 parameterizations.  Looking at coefficients for model 5, it's interesting that such a high fraction of the individuals fall into the group with larger sigma... was the study area small relative to bears home range size?  If so, you might expect a male-biased sample due to their greater movement rates, and hence a large number of animals in the 2nd mixture with larger sigma(?).

If you have a reasonable number of recaptures, results from models with and without individual heterogeneity shouldn't produce drastically different estimates. I think the low AIC weight and high and imprecise estimate of N from your model 3 is good evidence that the model doesn't fit your data well. I don't think that means that the a0 is better for modeling IH generally.  The parameter estimates for the effect of belonging to the second mixture in Howe et al. are quite precise and based on a large sample, and I also have a just so story that could explain the pattern we found... I'd like to think that we wouldn't have found support for the a0 parameterization with out data, but I can't be sure.

I agree that it would be nice to be able to try models with different pmix for the different parameters.

How small is your data set?  What is the ratio of detections to individuals?  Do you have the sex information?

All the best,
Eric

I am estimating densities of black bears and have run into some issues.

I initially attempted to model males and females differently (as in have different capthist files for males and females), but got similar density estimates for both. I thought maybe it would be worth a try to run sexes combined (single capthist file), but then still got densities that were similar for both sexes.

Would there be any reason why this happens? It would seem that males would typically be at lower densities.

I also attempted to run this data with auxiliary telemetry data in MARK and obtained estimates that were very different for males and females.

Roshan.

Hi Roshan
It won't help if your 'f'emale' models are fitted to male data, but I guess you didn't mean that! Your combined-sex model fits the same density for both groups - you need
sex.b2 <- secr.fit(bears, model = list(D~g, g0~g, sigma~g),
mask = bear.mask, groups="V5", method = 'Nelder-Mead', detectfn = 2,CL = F)
(I've taken the liberty of adding sigma~g). You could also try this to get a direct estimate of sex ratio (pmix) (see also ?hcov):
sex.b3 <- secr.fit(bears, model = list(g0~h2, sigma~h2),
mask = bear.mask, hcov="V5", method = 'Nelder-Mead', detectfn = 2,CL = F)
Murray

messages.subject: Re: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
messages.subject_clean: compensatory heterogeneity and finite mixture models
messages.body_plain:
OK, males only and plenty of recaptures...

My take on the finite mixtures is the coefficients are rarely "correct".  Detectability may vary among individuals due to many different factors; the two groups are forced because we use the 2-point mixture distribution to model the heterogeneity and may have no biological meaning at all.  When the coefficients for one of the mixtures really don't make sense (e.g. extremely low and imprecise g0 or sigma, as can occur with a high proportion of single captures), I usually conclude that the data "can't support" the mixture distribution and present estimates from a model that ignores heterogeneity, cautioning that D and N may have been underestimated and confidence interval coverage is likely less than nominal.  However, you seem to have both support for, and sufficient data to model, the heterogeneity.  Even if the coefficients don't correspond to real groups of animals, you can avoid negative bias and false precision by modeling the heterogeneity.

Even for your fairly large data set, you have included a lot of effects in your models.  Most effects are similar under different heterogeneity parameterizations, but we see that most of the parameter estimates change somewhat.  This situation makes it even riskier to try to infer too much from the coefficients, but I think it's reasonable to assume that your population estimates are useful (good chance that the true value is within the 95% CI), and in addition you've demonstrated some interesting effects (e.g. of area, in response to previous capture).  Will you be doing any model-averaging of the coefficients or abundance estimates?

Eric

messages.body_plain:
I replied to Eric, but forgot to reply all to the rest of the group.

I agree that we can't really interpret the two classes of the finite mixture model, but it's nice to have a biologically plausible explanation.  Of course these are easy to generate, so maybe they're not that useful.  The original cause for concern was finite mixture parameters that were inconsistent between g0 and a0 parameterizations.  When you increase sigma in the a0 parameterization, you indirectly decrease g0.  When you increase sigma in the g0 parameterization, you increase g0.  I fit these models to another male and female data set and it didn't produce the contradictory estimates.  In one case, there appeared to be some compensation and in the other case, not.  In the process, I managed to confuse myself about the original problem.  The original estimates are indeed contradictory.  Because of this and the poor performance of finite mixtures in small data sets with low capture probabilities in general, I think we'll ignore individual heterogeneity and say our estimates are probably conservative.  We are model averaging to shrink study area effects back towards a common mean.

None of these 3 data sets were very large.  I don't think you necessarily need a large data set to detect heterogeneity, but you may need a large data set to model it appropriately.  I wonder to what extent the Curse of Link remains in spatial mark recapture.  Instead of trying to correctly identify one heterogeneity distribution, we're now trying to correctly identify two potentially correlated random effects.

messages.subject_clean: group by detector covariates
messages.body_plain:
Hi
I think the catch is that density D may be modelled in 'secr' only using mask covariates defined for each point on a habitat mask and stored in the mask object (and some predefined predictors such as 'session' or 'g' for group). Trap covariates are defined only for each detector and are stored in the traps object. You might contrive to use the same covariate (e.g., GIS layer) to generate both a mask covariate and a detector covariate. User-defined distance functions open up some further possibilities for modelling sigma, but that gets more complex.
I hope this helps.
Murray
